sections.text:
News is coming over the mountains. “Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace!” For the peoples that Assyria crushed, it is the news they have waited for: the oppressor will not rise again.

Nahum announces the fall of Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian empire. He begins with who God is: “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power,” he says. Then, in vivid poetry, he lets the reader hear the city fall: the noise of the whip, the rattling wheels, horsemen charging, bodies without end. Its fortresses are like fig trees whose fruit drops into the mouth of the eater. Its defenses fail.

The city’s own cruelty is coming back upon it. The book ends on a question aimed at Nineveh: “who hasn’t felt your endless cruelty?”

The book was written between the fall of Thebes, an Egyptian city, in 663 before Christ, which it mentions, and the fall of Nineveh in 612. Assyria was known for the brutality of its conquests, and it had destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel a century earlier. Nahum himself is called the Elkoshite in the opening line.

Nahum is often read beside Jonah. In Jonah Nineveh repents and is spared. In Nahum, generations later, it faces judgment. Together they show God as both patient and just. The tone is harsh, and readers do well to remember who is speaking: the victims of an empire, hearing that its violence will end. Read that way, even its harshest lines belong to people who had suffered long and wanted to hear that it would end.
